summary: Defines TCP-ENO, a TCP option that lets two endpoints negotiate whether and how to encrypt a connection. It aims to help legacy protocols and applications that lack a signaling mechanism like STARTTLS get encryption deployed incrementally. It is experimental.

eli5.summary: Before two people talk, they agree to use a secret code. This is a way for two computers to say hello and agree to scramble their conversation, without changing the programs on top.

questions: how to negotiate encryption in tcp
how does tcp-eno work with legacy protocols
subtitle: Negotiating encryption at the TCP layer for legacy protocols and applications.

tldr.problem: Many TCP applications remain unencrypted because legacy protocols lack a signaling mechanism (like STARTTLS) to negotiate encryption, or applications cannot be upgraded and need encryption deployed transparently at the transport layer.
tldr.mechanism: TCP-ENO introduces a new TCP option (kind 69) that allows two endpoints to negotiate which TCP Encryption Protocol (TEP) to use during the three-way handshake. Both sides exchange lists of supported TEPs and agree on one, falling back to unencrypted TCP if negotiation fails.
tldr.outcome: Legacy and modern TCP applications can gain encryption without protocol-level changes, enabling incremental deployment of encryption across the Internet.

today: RFC 8547 is an Experimental specification published in May 2019. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and represents the primary standard for negotiating TCP-level encryption. Its experimental status reflects the need to gather data on middlebox behavior and deployment constraints before standardization.

sections.title: Introduction and Design Goals
sections.content:
Despite the growth of encrypted protocols like TLS, a significant portion of TCP traffic remains unencrypted. This persistence is due to two factors: legacy protocols lack a signaling mechanism by which to convey support for encryption (unlike STARTTLS in SMTP), and legacy applications cannot always be upgraded, requiring encryption to be deployed transparently within the transport layer.

RFC 8547 defines TCP-ENO (TCP Encryption Negotiation Option), a new TCP option that provides backward-compatible, out-of-band negotiation of encryption. The specification separates two questions: how to negotiate encryption at the TCP layer (ENO's job) and how to perform the actual encryption (delegated to separate TEP specifications). This separation enables future developments and supports multiple encryption protocols coexisting on the same path.
sections.eli5: TCP-ENO is a way for two computers to agree to encrypt their conversation right at the start, without needing the programs to know about it. If both support it, they encrypt; if one doesn't, they just talk normally.

sections.title: The ENO Option and Suboptions
sections.content:
TCP-ENO uses TCP option kind 69 to carry the negotiation. The ENO option contains suboptions that either offer support for a specific TCP Encryption Protocol (TEP) or provide global configuration. In SYN segments, the option lists available TEPs. In non-SYN segments, the option's presence acts as a one-bit acknowledgment that encryption negotiation is proceeding.

The first byte of each suboption encodes a type in the 7-bit glt field, with a high bit v indicating variable-length data. Global suboptions (glt values 0x00-0x1f) configure behavior like role assignment; TEP identifiers (glt values 0x20-0x7f) offer specific encryption protocols. A passive opener (typically a server) MUST include a global suboption with the passive role bit set to 1, while active openers default to 0.
sections.eli5: The ENO option is like a note that says 'I support encryption methods X, Y, and Z.' Each method gets a number from 0x20 upwards. The passive opener marks itself with a special bit so the other side knows who's who.

sections.title: The Handshake and Negotiation
sections.content:
TCP-ENO negotiation happens during the three-way handshake. The active opener sends a SYN segment containing an ENO option that lists supported TEPs. The passive opener receives this and responds with a SYN-ACK containing its own ENO option listing the TEPs it supports (typically just one, chosen from the active opener's list). The active opener completes the handshake with an ACK carrying a non-SYN-form ENO option to confirm receipt.

The negotiated TEP is determined as the last (highest-priority) valid TEP identifier that both sides offered. A TEP is valid when both sides sent a suboption for it and any suboption data satisfies the TEP's requirements. If no valid TEP exists—because no TEP is supported by both sides or role negotiation fails—the connection falls back to unencrypted TCP. This graceful fallback ensures backward compatibility: connections to endpoints that do not support TCP-ENO proceed normally without encryption.
sections.eli5: The active opener says 'I like methods X and Y.' The passive opener says 'I like Y.' Both sides agree on Y. If they disagree on methods or who's the server, they just give up and talk without encryption.

sections.title: Roles and Transcript Protection
sections.content:
To support operations that require distinguishing the two endpoints (such as endpoint authentication or asymmetric cipher negotiation), TCP-ENO defines two abstract roles: host A and host B. In normal client-server connections, the active opener is host A (role bit 0) and the passive opener is host B (role bit 1). In simultaneous open, one endpoint must explicitly configure its role bit to 1 for negotiation to succeed.

To defend against attacks that alter ENO options in transit, TEP specifications MUST incorporate a negotiation transcript into session IDs and authentication. This transcript consists of the TCP-ENO options exactly as they appeared in both sides' SYN segments, including kind and length bytes. By hashing this transcript, TEPs can detect and reject tampering. Additionally, each TEP MUST define a unique session ID of at least 33 bytes that identifies the connection, with all but the first byte being computationally indistinguishable from random to an eavesdropper.
sections.eli5: ENO uses an 'A' and 'B' system so both sides know who is who. It also saves a fingerprint of the negotiation so if someone changes it on the way, both sides will notice and the encryption won't work.

sections.title: Security Considerations and TEP Requirements
sections.content:
TCP-ENO supports both opportunistic encryption (no endpoint authentication) and stronger security (with endpoint authentication). Opportunistic encryption protects against undetectable large-scale eavesdropping but not against active attacks like man-in-the-middle. For stronger security, applications MUST incorporate session IDs into endpoint authentication mechanisms.

To ensure interoperability and security, every TEP claiming an ENO TEP identifier MUST satisfy strict requirements: use authenticated encryption (AEAD), protect TCP flags and urgent data, guarantee stream confidentiality without assuming long-lived secrets, provide forward secrecy, and never allow null cipher suites. TEPs MUST also use encryption algorithms with at least 120 bits of security strength. Implementations MUST have access to adequate randomness before sending ENO options, as weak randomness undermines the security of the entire system.
sections.eli5: TCP-ENO by itself doesn't prove who you're talking to, so apps need to authenticate each other separately. Every encryption method must be strong (no weak ciphers), must scramble everything, and must forget old secrets quickly.
